stories.title_en: A Cunning Broker Dumps Paper and Pays with His Daughter

paragraphs.zh: 施守训，福建大安人。家资殷富，常造纸卖客。一日，自装千餘篓，价值八百餘两，往苏州卖，寓牙人翁滨二店。滨乃宿牙，叠积前客债甚多，见施雏商，将其纸尽还前客，误施坐候半年。家中又发纸五百餘篓到苏州，滨代现卖。付银讫，托言系取旧帐者，复候半年。知受其笼络，施乃怒骂殴之。滨无言可应，当凭乡亲刘光前议，谕滨立过借批银八百两，劝施暂回。
paragraphs.en: Shi Shouxun was a man of Da’an in Fujian. His household was wealthy; he often made paper and sold it to merchants. One day he packed more than a thousand baskets, worth over eight hundred taels, went to Suzhou to sell, and lodged at the shop of the broker Weng Bin’er. Bin was a veteran broker, stacked with many debts to earlier clients. Seeing Shi was a greenhorn merchant, he used all the paper to repay previous clients, and kept Shi waiting half a year. The household then sent another five hundred-odd baskets of paper to Suzhou; Bin sold them for ready money. After the silver was paid over, he claimed it was for collecting old accounts, and Shi waited another half year. Knowing he had been snared, Shi then cursed and beat him. Bin had no words to answer. On the mediation of fellow-townsman Liu Guangqian, they instructed Bin to write a loan note for eight hundred taels of silver, and advised Shi to go home for the time being.

paragraphs.zh: 次年，复载纸到苏州，滨代现卖。只前帐难还，施又坐待半年。见其女云英有貌，未曾许配，思此银难取，乃浼刘光前为媒，求其女为妾，抵还前帐。滨悦许之。其女年方十五，执不肯从。滨与妻入劝曰：“古有缇萦愿没官为婢，以赎父罪。今父欠客人银八百两，以汝填还；况福建客家多巨富，若后日生子，分其家财，居此致富，享福非小。”女始允诺。时施已六十餘矣。成婚近四载，施后回家身故。未及周期服，滨将女重嫁南京溧水县梁恩赐为妾，重收聘礼一百两。
paragraphs.en: The next year Shi again loaded paper to Suzhou; Bin sold it for ready money. Only the old account was hard to repay, and Shi waited another half year. He saw Bin’s daughter Yunying was pretty and not yet betrothed. Thinking this silver would be hard to collect, he asked Liu Guangqian to act as matchmaker, seeking the daughter as a concubine to offset the old account. Bin gladly agreed. The girl was just fifteen and firmly would not consent. Bin and his wife went in and advised her: “In ancient times Tiying was willing to become an official slave to redeem her father’s crime. Now Father owes a client eight hundred taels; we fill it with you. Besides, Fujian merchant houses are often very rich. If later you bear a son and share the family wealth, you will live here in riches and enjoy no small fortune.” The girl then agreed. Shi was already over sixty. They were married nearly four years; later Shi went home and died. Before a full year of mourning, Bin remarried the girl as concubine to Liang Enci of Lishui county, Nanjing, and again took a betrothal gift of one hundred taels.

paragraphs.zh: 守训男施钦知之为，本年亦装纸到苏州，往拜翁家，呼翁为“外祖”。翁不瞅睬他。请庶母出见，亦拒不出。众客伙皆怒而嗾曰：“你父以八百两聘礼，止成亲四载，未期服又重嫁他人。今一出见何害？情甚可恶！汝何不鸣官？”钦乃告于巡街蔡御史。时翁滨二得施为婿，复振家风，又发资金千餘，见告，毫无惧意。两下各投分上，讦讼几二年。各司道皆纳分上，附会而判。后钦状告刑部，始获公断曰：“翁滨二以女抵偿八百两，几与绿珠同价矣。但守训自肯，其财礼勿论。今夫服未满重嫁梁客，兜重财物，是以女为货，不顾律法。合责三十板，断身资银一百两，并守训为云英置衣资首饰银五十两，共与施钦领之。”因此积讼连年，滨二之家财尽倾，仍流落于贫矣。
paragraphs.en: Shouxun’s son Shi Qin learned of this. That same year he also packed paper to Suzhou, went to pay respects at the Weng house, and called Weng “maternal grandfather.” Weng paid him no attention. He asked to have his stepmother come out to see him; she also refused to come out. Fellow merchants were all angry and egged him on: “Your father paid eight hundred taels as betrothal, were husband and wife only four years, and before mourning was complete she was remarried to someone else. What harm is there in coming out once to see you? The feeling is hateful! Why not report it to the officials?” Qin then accused him before Street-Patrolling Censor Cai. By then Weng Bin’er, having gained Shi as a son-in-law, had revived the family style and put out over a thousand more in capital; seeing the accusation, he had not the slightest fear. Both sides used connections and sued for nearly two years. All the circuit and provincial offices took bribes and judged by stretching the facts. Later Qin filed with the Ministry of Justice, and only then got a fair judgment: “Weng Bin’er offset eight hundred taels with his daughter—almost the same price as Lüzhu, the famously costly concubine. But Shouxun consented of his own will; we will not discuss the betrothal wealth. Now, before the husband’s mourning was complete, she was remarried to merchant Liang, scooping up more goods—this is treating a daughter as merchandise, with no regard for the law. He should be beaten thirty strokes; we award body-price silver of one hundred taels, plus the fifty taels Shouxun spent on clothes and ornaments for Yunying, all to be received by Shi Qin.” Because of years of piled-up lawsuits, Bin’er’s family wealth was entirely gone, and he fell back into poverty.

paragraphs.zh: 按：脱骗之害，首侠棍，次狡侩。侠棍设局暗脱，窃盗也。狡侩骗货明卖，强盗也。二者当与盗同科。凡牙侩之弊，客货入店，彼皆作纲抵偿，又多窃取供家，每以后客货盖前客帐，此穷牙常态也。施守训在不早审牙家，致落此坑堑。只可小心逼取，或继以告，不当图其女为妾。夫以六旬上人，岁月几何，纳妾异地，能无后患乎？贻子后讼，所费不资。虽最终取胜，得不偿失矣。独恨翁滨二负心歹汉，以一女而还银八百两，得已过分，又得婿扶以成家；后女虽再嫁，当以身资还施之男，永可无患矣。乃贪心不满，再致倾家，真可为欺心负义之鉴。
paragraphs.en: Note: Among the harms of stripping and swindling, first come swaggering ruffians, then cunning brokers. Swaggering ruffians set traps and strip in the dark—that is theft. Cunning brokers cheat you of goods and sell them in the open—that is robbery. Both should be punished like bandits. As for the tricks of brokers: once a client’s goods enter the shop, they use them as a batch to offset debts, and also steal much for household use; they always cover earlier clients’ accounts with later clients’ goods. This is the usual way of a poor broker. Shi Shouxun’s fault was not checking the broker’s house early, so he fell into this pit. He should only have pressed carefully for payment, or followed with a lawsuit; he should not have schemed to take the daughter as concubine. A man past sixty—how many years does he have left? Taking a concubine in a strange place—can there be no later trouble? He left his son a later lawsuit, and the costs were enormous. Though he finally won, the gain did not cover the loss. What is hateful is Weng Bin’er, a heartless scoundrel: with one daughter he repaid eight hundred taels, already more than enough, and then got a son-in-law’s help to rebuild the household. Later, even if the girl remarried, he should have given the body-price back to Shi’s son, and there would have been no trouble forever. But his greedy heart was not satisfied, and he brought on the ruin of his house. Truly a mirror for those who cheat the heart and betray duty.

stories.title_en: A Poor Broker Dumps Wax to Pay Old Debts

paragraphs.zh: 张霸，四川人。为人机关精密，身长力勇。一日，买蜡百餘担，往福建建宁府丘店发卖。此牙家盆彻骨，外张富态，欠前客货银极多。霸蜡到，即以光棍顶作鬼名来借蜡，约后还银。数日后，霸往街游玩，其蜡遍在诸铺。及问其姓名，皆与帐名不同。霸心疑必有弊，故回店讯问牙人曰：“你脱我蜡去还前帐，可一一实报帐来。若不实言，你乘我几拳不得。”丘牙哑口无应。霸轮拳擒打，如鹰擒雀，如踢戏球。丘牙连忙求饶，曰：“公神人也。此蜡真还前客旧帐，并家用去矣，何能问各店重取？”张霸曰：“你将还人的及各店买去的，都登上帐，只说他揭借去，俱未还银。我将帐去告，取你硬作证，怕他各店不再还我？”丘牙依言，一一写成发货帐。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba was a man of Sichuan. His schemes were fine and close; he was tall and strong. One day he bought more than a hundred loads of wax and went to sell it at the Qiu shop in Jianning Prefecture, Fujian. This broker’s house was poor to the bone, but outwardly put on a rich look, and owed a great deal of silver for earlier clients’ goods. When Ba’s wax arrived, they had ruffians come under dummy names to “borrow” the wax, promising to pay silver later. A few days later Ba walked the streets for amusement, and his wax was in shops all over. When he asked their names, none matched the names on the account. Ba suspected there must be a trick, so he went back to the shop and questioned the broker: “You dumped my wax to pay old accounts. Report the accounts one by one, truthfully. If you do not tell the truth, you will not get away with a few of my punches.” Broker Qiu was dumbstruck. Ba swung his fists and beat him, like a hawk seizing a sparrow, like kicking a play-ball. Qiu hurriedly begged for mercy: “You are a spirit, sir. This wax truly went to pay earlier clients’ old accounts, and for household use besides. How can I go to the shops and take it back?” Zhang Ba said: “Put down on the account what you repaid people and what the shops bought; just say they took it on credit and have not yet paid the silver. I will take the account and file a complaint, and have you firmly testify. Are you afraid those shops will not pay me again?” Qiu followed his words and wrote out the dispatch-of-goods account one by one.

paragraphs.zh: 张霸即具状告府。署印梅爷看状，掷地不准。霸心伤失本，两眼自然垂。再三哀告，梅爷乃准其状。先差皂隶往查各店蜡。霸以银贿公差，回报曰：“各店果有张霸印号蜡。”梅爷曰：“哪有揭借客蜡都不还银者！”即出牌拘审。
paragraphs.en: Zhang Ba then filed a complaint at the prefecture. Acting prefect Master Mei looked at the complaint, threw it on the ground, and would not accept it. Ba was wounded at heart over losing his capital; tears fell of themselves. After he pleaded again and again, Master Mei accepted the complaint. He first sent yamen runners to check the wax in the shops. Ba bribed the runners with silver; they reported back: “The shops do indeed have wax with Zhang Ba’s stamp.” Master Mei said: “How can there be people who take a client’s wax on credit and never pay the silver!” He issued a warrant to arrest and try them.

paragraphs.zh: 各店在外商量曰：“我店买张客蜡，俱已还银，牙家收讫。又牙人自用蜡还我者，是他所合抽得牙钱，何得今更重告？吾与汝等敛银共用，投一分上，先去讲明，然后对审。”敛银已毕，即将银一百两投梅爷乡亲。
paragraphs.en: The shops conferred outside: “Our shops bought merchant Zhang’s wax and have already paid the silver; the broker received it. And the wax the broker himself used to repay us was what he had as his brokerage cut. How can he now sue us again? Let us pool silver to use together, send a connection in first to explain, then confront them at trial.” When the silver was collected, they sent one hundred taels to a fellow-townsman of Master Mei.

paragraphs.zh: 梅爷刚正之官，弗听，即拘来审。内有江店客人，乃惯讼者，先对理曰：“蜡乃丘牙明卖与我，公平交易，张霸安得重取？即未全交付，亦牙家刻落，与我辈何干？”丘牙曰：“蜡非卖他。是小人先欠诸店旧帐，张霸蜡到，他等诈言措借，数日后即还银。及得蜡到手，即坐以抵前帐。非小人敢兜客银也。”梅爷曰：“丘牙欠债，须问彼自取，安得坐客人货以还彼债？你众等可将价还张霸，免你等罪。”江店恃有分上，再三辩论，说是明白交易，并无对债之事。梅爷触怒，将江店责十板；江店又辩论不已，又被责二十板。后诸人惊惧，皆称愿赔求饶。以江店监禁，诸人讨保，断蜡银，限三日，不完再重责。三日果追完。霸领银讫，深感梅爷恩泽，顶戴香炉，到于堂下，叩拜而去。
paragraphs.en: Master Mei was an upright official and would not listen. He had them brought for trial. Among them was a client of the Jiang shop, used to lawsuits, who first argued: “The wax was openly sold to me by broker Qiu, a fair deal. How can Zhang Ba take it a second time? Even if it was not fully handed over, that is the broker’s skimming—what has it to do with us?” Broker Qiu said: “The wax was not sold to them. This humble person first owed the shops old accounts. When Zhang Ba’s wax arrived, they falsely said they would borrow it and pay silver in a few days. Once they had the wax in hand, they sat on it to offset the old accounts. It is not that this humble person dared pocket the client’s silver.” Master Mei said: “If broker Qiu owes debts, they should collect from him. How can they sit on a client’s goods to repay his debts? You lot will pay the price to Zhang Ba, and I will spare you punishment.” The Jiang shop, relying on the connection, argued again and again that it was a clear sale, with no offsetting of debts. Master Mei was angered, beat the Jiang shop ten strokes; Jiang still would not stop arguing, and was beaten another twenty. Then the others were frightened and all said they were willing to pay and begged for mercy. Jiang was jailed; the others found guarantors. The wax silver was judged due in three days; if not complete, they would be heavily beaten again. In three days it was indeed collected in full. Ba received the silver, deeply grateful for Master Mei’s kindness; he wore an incense brazier on his head, went before the hall, kowtowed, and left.

paragraphs.zh: 按：出外为商，以缥缈之身，涉寡亲之境，全仗经纪以为耳目。若遇经纪公正，则货物有主；一投狡侩，而抑货亏价必矣。是择经纪，乃经商一大关系也，可不慎哉！如其人言谈直率，此是公正之人。若初会晤间，上下估看，方露微言，则其心中狡猾可知。若价即言而不远，应对迟慢，心必怀欺。若屋宇精致，分外巧样，多是奢华务外之人，内必不能积聚。倘衣补垢腻，人鄙形猥，肩耸目光，巾帽不称寒暑，此皆贫穷之辈。若巧异妆扮，服色变常，必非创置之人，其内必无财钞。若衣冠不华，惟服布衣，此乃老实本分，不可以斯之曰贫。商而知此，何至如张霸，被牙所脱也？况非刚正之梅爷，肯听分上，几乎素手归矣。故录之，以示为商者。当货物发脱之初，细审经纪对手，发落方可保无虞矣。
paragraphs.en: Note: When you go out as a merchant, a body adrift in a place with few kin, you rely entirely on the broker as your eyes and ears. If you meet an honest broker, the goods have a master; once you fall in with a cunning broker, the goods will be held down and the price shorted, that is certain. So choosing a broker is a great matter in trade—can you not be careful? If a man’s talk is straight and frank, he is an honest man. If at the first meeting he looks you up and down, and only then lets out a few words, you can tell his mind is sly. If he names a price at once and it is not far off, but answers slowly, his heart must hold deceit. If the house is finely built, extra-clever in style, he is likely a man of luxury who tends to outward show, and inwardly cannot accumulate. If his clothes are patched and greasy, his person mean and his form ugly, shoulders hunched and eyes staring, cap and kerchief not matching the season—these are all the poor. If he dresses in odd, clever ways, colors and clothes out of the ordinary, he is surely not a man who has built anything up, and inwardly he has no cash. If his cap and gown are not showy, and he wears only cloth, this is an honest, proper man; you cannot call him poor on that account. If a merchant knows this, how would he come to be like Zhang Ba, stripped by a broker? Besides, if it had not been the upright Master Mei, who refused to hear connections, he would nearly have gone home empty-handed. So I record this to show merchants: at the very start when goods are to be sold off, look closely at the broker you deal with; only then can you dispatch the goods without worry.
